MScFE 610 Financial Econometrics — Group Work Project 2¶

BTC Econometrics Lab · Group 8665¶

Team: Kow Kai Sheng (Malaysia) · Ajeet Kumar (India) · Faith Nyaboe Momanyi (Kenya)

Challenges addressed: (1) non-stationarity and finding an equilibrium, (2) detecting a regime change, (3) handling multicollinearity, (4) feature extraction.

Asset: BTC-USD daily, 2020-01-01 → 2025-02-27 (Yahoo Finance). A genuinely cointegrated second pair (Alphabet's GOOGL / GOOG dual-class shares) is added so the equilibrium/ECM section has a valid positive example, not only a rejection.

This is the corrected notebook. Every defect found in the original submission is fixed and flagged inline with FIX: comments. The companion file report/REVIEW.md lists all of them with before/after evidence.

1. Non-stationarity and finding an equilibrium¶

Definition¶

Augmented Dickey–Fuller (H₀: a unit root is present)

$$\Delta y_t=\alpha+\beta t+\phi y_{t-1}+\sum_{i=1}^{p}\gamma_i\Delta y_{t-i}+\varepsilon_t$$

KPSS (H₀: the series is stationary), with $y_t=\mu+\delta t+R_t+\varepsilon_t$ and $R_t$ a random walk

$$\eta=\frac{1}{T^{2}}\cdot\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T}S_t^{2}}{\hat\sigma^{2}},\qquad S_t=\sum_{i=1}^{t}\hat\varepsilon_i$$

Engle–Granger cointegration: estimate $y_t=\alpha+\beta x_t+\epsilon_t$ by OLS, then test $\hat\epsilon_t$ for a unit root using MacKinnon cointegration critical values.

Error-correction model

$$\Delta y_t=\alpha+\phi\,(y_{t-1}-\hat\beta x_{t-1})+\gamma\Delta x_t+\varepsilon_t,\qquad \phi<0$$

VAR(p)

$$\mathbf{z}_t=\mathbf{c}+\sum_{i=1}^{p}\mathbf{A}_i\mathbf{z}_{t-i}+\mathbf{u}_t$$

Description¶

A price level is typically I(1); its first difference or return is I(0). Two I(1) series are cointegrated when some linear combination is I(0), which defines a long-run equilibrium toward which the system is pulled. The ECM's $\phi$ measures the daily speed of that pull.

FIX 5: KPSS p-values are bounded, and the two tests must be read jointly¶

statsmodels truncates KPSS p-values to $[0.01, 0.10]$. The original printed p: 0.1 as if it were exact; we report the bound. We also classify each series by the joint ADF/KPSS outcome.

FIX 6: the integration order of the partner series was never checked¶

This is decisive. Cointegration is defined between series of the same order, normally I(1).

In [4]:
orders = [stn.integration_order(d, 'Close'), stn.integration_order(d, 'Volume')]
pd.DataFrame(orders)

Demonstration — Engle–Granger on BTC close vs volume¶

FIX 7: wrong critical values¶

The original ran a plain adfuller on the OLS residuals and read off the ordinary Dickey–Fuller p-value. Residual-based cointegration tests need MacKinnon's values, which statsmodels.tsa.stattools.coint supplies — a function the original notebook imported but never called.

FIX 8: unbalanced regression¶

Close is I(1) but Volume is already stationary in levels, so this is not a cointegration problem at all. The correct verdict is "precondition violated", not merely "no cointegration".

In [5]:
eg = stn.engle_granger(d, 'Close', 'Volume')
print(eg['ols'].summary())
print(f"\nPrecondition (both I(1)) satisfied: {eg['precondition_ok']}")
print(f"naive ADF p-value on residuals : {eg['naive_adf_p']:.5f}   <- what the original reported")
print(f"correct Engle-Granger p-value  : {eg['eg_p']:.5f}   <- MacKinnon critical values")
print('EG critical values:', {k: round(v,3) for k,v in eg['eg_crit'].items()})
print(f"R2 = {eg['r2']:.4f} | Durbin-Watson = {eg['dw']:.4f} | cointegrated = {eg['cointegrated']}")

Diagnosis¶

The levels regression is spurious in the Granger–Newbold sense: $R^2=0.101$ looks like a finding, but the Durbin–Watson statistic of $0.074$ is almost zero and the residual carries a unit root (EG $p=0.957$). The condition number of $7.7\times10^{10}$ is a units problem, not evidence of multicollinearity — a single regressor cannot be collinear with itself.

Demonstration — ECM (and why it must be gated)¶

FIX 9: an ECM was fitted without cointegration¶

By the Granger representation theorem an ECM is only valid if the pair is cointegrated. The original fitted one anyway and then explained the insignificant $\phi$ as a modelling failure.

Directions — a pair that genuinely is cointegrated¶

Alphabet's GOOGL (voting) and GOOG (non-voting) shares are claims on the same cash flows, so no-arbitrage predicts a log-price hedge ratio near 1 and a stationary spread. This gives the assignment a valid equilibrium and a working ECM.

In [8]:
g1, _ = data.get_data('GOOGL'); g2, _ = data.get_data('GOOG')
p1, p2 = data.prepare(g1, 'GOOGL'), data.prepare(g2, 'GOOG')
pair = pd.concat([p1['Close'].rename('GOOGL'), p2['Close'].rename('GOOG')], axis=1).dropna()

eg2 = stn.engle_granger(pair, 'GOOGL', 'GOOG', log=True)
ecm2 = stn.fit_ecm(eg2, pair, 'GOOGL', 'GOOG', log=True)
print(f"n = {eg2['n']} | both I(1): {eg2['precondition_ok']}")
print(f"hedge ratio beta = {eg2['beta']:.4f}  (theory predicts ~1)")
print(f"Engle-Granger p  = {eg2['eg_p']:.5f} -> cointegrated: {eg2['cointegrated']}")
print(ecm2['model'].summary())
print(f"\nphi = {ecm2['phi']:.5f} (p = {ecm2['phi_p']:.2e})")
print(f"{abs(ecm2['phi'])*100:.2f}% of the gap closes per day; half-life = {ecm2['half_life_days']:.1f} days")

Demonstration — VAR on stationary, scale-matched differences¶

FIX 10: the lag cap was arbitrary and binding¶

max_lags = min(15, n-1) made AIC/HQIC/FPE all select exactly 15 — the cap, not an interior optimum. We use the Schwert rule $\lfloor 12(n/100)^{1/4}\rfloor$ and prefer the parsimonious BIC.

FIX 11: no diagnostics were run¶

We add the stability check, a Portmanteau whiteness test and Granger causality.

In [10]:

Diagnosis / Damage / Directions / Deployment (Challenge 1)¶

  • Diagnosis. Price levels are I(1); returns are I(0). BTC close and volume are not cointegrated, and the regression is unbalanced because volume is I(0). The VAR is stable but its residuals are not white (Portmanteau $p\approx10^{-9}$), so linear dynamics remain unmodelled.
  • Damage. Using the levels regression for hedging or forecasting would be a classic spurious- regression error. An ECM built on it has no error-correction mechanism.
  • Directions. Model returns, not dollar levels; use a genuinely cointegrated pair (GOOGL/GOOG) for equilibrium work; extend the VAR (or move to a GARCH-in-mean / VARMA specification) until residuals are white.
  • Deployment. The GOOGL/GOOG spread is a live statistical-arbitrage signal: enter when the gap exceeds a threshold, expect reversion with a ~12-day half-life, and re-test cointegration monthly because the relationship can break.

2. Detecting a regime change¶

Definition¶

$$y_t=\mu_{S_t}+\epsilon_t,\qquad \epsilon_t\sim N(0,\sigma^2_{S_t}),\qquad P(S_t=j\mid S_{t-1}=i)=p_{ij}$$ $$\mathbb{E}[\text{duration of regime } i]=\frac{1}{1-p_{ii}}$$

Description¶

An unobserved Markov chain switches the mean and variance between a calm and a turbulent state. The Hamilton filter/smoother recovers $P(S_t=j\mid y_1,\dots,y_T)$.

FIX 12 — the most serious defect in the submission¶

The original code did:

df['Regime'] = regime_result.predict()

and the report then wrote "the regime values (20–60) likely correspond to the probability (%) of being in Regime 1 … a value of 60 implies a 60% probability".

predict() returns the conditional mean of the series in dollars, a probability-weighted average of the regime means. It is not a label and not a probability. The observed 20–60 range is simply the two fitted means (21.06 and 58.79). Correct inference uses smoothed_marginal_probabilities.

FIX 13 — dollar differences make regimes track the price level¶

BTC rose from ~$7k to ~$90k, so a constant percentage move becomes a much larger dollar move. A regime model on dollar differences therefore confuses the price level with risk.

FIX 14 — single-start optimisation¶

Markov likelihoods are multimodal; we run a multi-start search and keep the best log-likelihood.

In [12]:

print('ORIGINAL SPECIFICATION: dollar differences')
print(f"predict() ranges {mk_dollar['predict_range'][0]:.2f} to {mk_dollar['predict_range'][1]:.2f} DOLLARS")
print('  -> these are the regime means, not probabilities')

Diagnosis¶

The dollar specification calls 2021 turbulent on 100% of days and 2024–25 on ~95%, while labelling the March-2020 crash calm on 93% of days. That is economically backwards and is purely a price-level artefact. On percent returns the turbulent share is 25% in 2020, peaks at 44% in 2021 and is lowest in 2023 (13%).

Caveat (second review pass). The fitted chain has expected durations of only ~4.1 (calm) and ~2.3 (turbulent) days and switches 485 times in 1,884 days. At daily frequency a two-state model is mostly separating ordinary days from fat-tail days — a mixture of normals, i.e. volatility clustering — not a set of persistent structural regimes. The yearly shares are a descriptive flag; GARCH is the better tool for forecasting risk.

The corrected model gives $\sigma_{\text{calm}}=1.65\%$/day and $\sigma_{\text{turb}}=5.09\%$/day, a 3.1× ratio, with expected durations of about 4.1 and 2.3 days.

Two further report contradictions are resolved: the turbulent regime has a higher fitted mean (+0.38% vs +0.08%), not "significant negative price changes"; and both variance parameters are significant at $p<0.001$, so the claim that "variance differences do not show statistical significance" is incorrect.

Damage¶

Sizing positions from dollar-based regimes would have cut risk in the calm 2020 window and kept full risk through 2024–25 — the opposite of what the volatility actually warranted.

Directions¶

Model returns; allow 3 regimes or a switching mean-and-variance specification; add macro covariates; validate against realised volatility rather than the model's own labels.

Deployment¶

Publish the daily smoothed $P(\text{turbulent})$; de-risk when it crosses 0.5 and hold the reduced exposure for the expected regime duration (~2–4 days), re-estimating monthly.

3. Handling multicollinearity¶

Definition¶

$$\mathrm{VIF}_j=\frac{1}{1-R_j^{2}}$$ where $R_j^2$ comes from regressing predictor $j$ on all the other predictors. VIF > 10 is severe.

Description¶

Near-duplicate predictors inflate coefficient standard errors, so individual effects become insignificant and unstable even when the fit looks acceptable.

FIX 15 — the original test could not detect anything¶

VIF was computed on Diff_Close and Diff_Volume: the two dependent variables of the VAR, which are not regressors of one another. VIF ≈ 1.001 was guaranteed by construction. A VIF was also reported for the intercept, which is meaningless.

FIX 16 — PCA on unstandardised data¶

Volume (~1e10) dwarfs price changes (~1e2), so "PC1 explains 100%" was a units artefact. The report then contradicted itself, claiming both "one dominant factor showing alignment" and "no redundant information". Standardising removes the artefact.

FIX 17 — look-ahead bias¶

A moving-average gap built as rolling(w).mean()/Close - 1 contains today's return, because today's close is in the denominator. Every predictor here is lagged one day.

Diagnosis / Damage / Directions / Deployment (Challenge 3)¶

  • Diagnosis. With a realistic predictor set the pathology is unmistakable: ma10_gap VIF ≈ 27.6, ma20_gap ≈ 18.6, ma50_gap ≈ 12.5. Only a minority of coefficients is significant and in-sample $R^2$ is below 1%.
  • Damage. Individually insignificant, sign-unstable coefficients invite false narratives about which indicator "drives" returns. OLS is nominally the worst of the four candidates, but the best remedy beats it by only 0.04–0.66% out of sample, and Ridge picks the largest penalty on its (widened) grid — it shrinks every slope towards zero. Fixing collinearity does not create predictability here.
  • Directions. Standardise before PCA; trim redundant windows; use Ridge or principal-component regression. Three components already carry ~85% of the predictor variance.
  • Deployment. Ship the regularised model, not the kitchen-sink OLS. Re-check VIF whenever a feature is added, and re-select the Ridge penalty on a rolling window.

4. Feature extraction¶

Definition¶

Conditional mean (ARMA(p,q)): $$r_t=c+\sum_{i=1}^{p}\phi_i r_{t-i}+\sum_{j=1}^{q}\theta_j\varepsilon_{t-j}+\varepsilon_t$$ Conditional variance (GARCH(1,1)): $$\sigma_t^{2}=\omega+\alpha\varepsilon_{t-1}^{2}+\beta\sigma_{t-1}^{2},\qquad \omega>0,\ \alpha,\beta\ge0$$ Persistence $\alpha+\beta<1$ is required for a finite unconditional variance $\bar\sigma^2=\omega/(1-\alpha-\beta)$; the volatility half-life is $\ln(0.5)/\ln(\alpha+\beta)$. Squared return $r_t^2$ is a noisy but unbiased proxy for realised variance. Kalman local level: $r_t=\mu_t+\varepsilon_t$, $\mu_t=\mu_{t-1}+\eta_t$.

Description¶

Raw prices are noisy and non-stationary. Returns, an ARMA conditional mean, a GARCH conditional variance, squared returns and a Kalman-smoothed level compress the series into a few informative, comparably-scaled features.

FIX 19 — scaling decided the economic conclusion¶

arch warned DataScaleWarning: the scale of y is 0.001099. The original ignored it and obtained $\alpha=0.673$, $\beta=0.036$ (persistence 0.71), then concluded "baseline level volatility … the GARCH has not fully captured the volatility spikes". On percent returns with rescale=False, every t-error specification is extremely persistent (0.99–1.00; normal-error GARCH 0.97) — shocks to volatility decay very slowly. Note that arch constrains α+β ≤ 1, so the exact 1.000 for GARCH-t is the optimiser sitting on its bound; the unconstrained EGARCH-t (persistence 0.99, best AIC) is the better evidence. The original conclusion was an optimiser artefact.

FIX 20 — double mean, mislabelled plot, duplicated show()¶

The original fitted ARIMA, then fitted arch_model on its residuals, which adds a second constant mean. The plot title said ARIMA(1,1,1) while the model was (1,0,1), and a duplicated plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() emitted an empty figure.

Diagnosis / Damage / Directions / Deployment (Challenge 4)¶

  • Diagnosis. Returns are stationary (ADF $p\approx3\times10^{-26}$). Volatility is near-integrated: $\alpha+\beta=1.000$ for GARCH-t (the optimiser's bound) and 0.99 for EGARCH-t, so the unconditional variance is effectively undefined and shocks fade very slowly. The Student-t tail index $\nu\approx3.1$ confirms very heavy tails; EGARCH-t wins on AIC. The Kalman signal-to-noise ratio is ~1e-5, i.e. no persistent drift.
  • Damage. With $\nu\approx3$ a normal model understates the 99% tail (≈6.4% vs ≈7.3% one-day VaR); at 95% the Student-t VaR (≈3.8%) is actually smaller than the normal one (≈4.5%) because the standardised t concentrates more mass near the centre. Near-integration implies variance forecasts barely mean-revert, so long-horizon risk cannot be anchored to a historical average. The earlier "no volatility clustering" reading was simply wrong.
  • Directions. Prefer EGARCH-t on AIC; consider a component/FIGARCH model to separate transitory from permanent volatility; re-estimate on a rolling window; validate VaR with Kupiec and Christoffersen backtests.
  • Deployment (illustrative, not advice). Publish the daily volatility term structure and t-based 95%/99% VaR; monitor breaches of the 1-day 99% VaR as a model-health check.
